catalog_quote: Accentuation. In general, dissyllables and trisyllables accent the first syllable; as, puntimai, 'a messenger'; piriwal, 'a chief or king.' Compound derivative words, being descriptive nouns, have the accent universally on the last syllable; as, wiyellikan, 'one who speaks,' from wiyelli, 'the action of speaking' ... Verbs in the present and the past tenses have their accent on those parts of the verb which are significant of these tenses; as, tatan, 'eats'; wiyan, 'speaks'; wiya, 'hath told.' This must be particularly attended to; else a mere affirmation will become an imperative, and so on ... In the future tenses, the accent is always on the last syllable but one, whether the word consists of two syllables or of more; as, tanun, 'shall or will eat' ... Present participles have the accent on the last syllable; as, bunkillin, 'now in the action of smiting'; wiyellin, 'now in the action…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated place in the held 1892 text (Grammar pp. 2-3, 'Accentuation' then 'Emphasis'). (2) The classification rests on a first-hand 1834 missionary grammar sketch via its 1892 re-edition; for a language with no speakers since the 19th century this is the authoritative primary record, and the modern salvage grammar (Lissarrague 2006, held) has no independent stress analysis and reads Threlkeld's accent as stress marking past tense (p. 73), consistent with 'morphological'. sources.citation: Hale, Horatio. 1846. Ethnography and Philology (United States Exploring Expedition, vol. VI). Philadelphia: Lea and Blanchard. 'The languages of Australia', pp. 479ff (grammar of the Lake Macquarie language, which Hale labels 'Kamilarai', from Threlkeld's materials plus Hale's own 1839-40 visit). (archive.org Ethnographyphil00Hale)
sources.quote: pp. 482-483: 'The accent, in words of two syllables, is usually on the first, and in words of three or more on the antepenultimate; but to this there are many exceptions.' p. 485: nouns 'in ro, belonging to the fifth [declension], require the accent to be shifted to the o, as makoro, fish, active nominative, makaro.'
sources.locator: pp. 482-483 (general phonology of the two NSW languages described); p. 485 (declensions)
